transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess since I stopped working, I just can’t seem to slow myself down. I’m retired now, but I’m still up and moving all day, going from one little job to the next, like there’s still a crew waiting on me somewhere. I’ll start doing one thing, then notice something else, and next thing I know I’ve been on my feet all day. It’s been wearing on me some, and I figured I should come in and talk about it.
Do you often act on impulse without thinking things through?

Yeah, I do sometimes. Like in the storytelling group I go to, somebody will be halfway through saying something and I’ll jump in with my answer or my own thought before they’re done. I don’t mean to be rude—half the time I’m just excited because it reminds me of something, like one old work story leads to another—but then I see I cut them off and I feel bad about it.
Do you have trouble focusing on one task for a long period of time?

Yeah, I do. If I’m trying to paint something, or sit down and plan out a story for that group, I’ll be going along fine and then I hear a truck outside—could be the delivery guy, could be just someone backing up—and my mind is out the window. Or I’ll suddenly think, “Oh, I should check the garden,” and then I’ve lost the thread of what I was doing. It’s not that I don’t want to finish it, I just sort of… jump tracks.
Were you very active or restless when you were a child?

Oh yeah, I think so. Even back in grade school, teachers would say I was bright enough, but scattered. I was always losing pencils—my mother used to get so annoyed buying more—and I’d call out answers before I was supposed to. They were always reminding me to finish my work before running out to recess. Funny, I can still picture those old wooden desks… but yes, I was restless in that way, even then.
Do you often feel overly frustrated or irritable when things don't go as planned?

I’m not sure I’d say “overly,” exactly. I mean, I get annoyed like anyone does—if something I planned doesn’t happen, I’ll grumble a bit. Like when I think I’m going to get to something in the yard and then the weather turns, that kind of thing. Though last week I was out there fussing with the hose and ended up noticing the fence needs fixing, and then I forgot why I went out there in the first place…

But, uh, frustration—yeah, I don’t know. I wouldn’t say it’s a big thing I’ve really noticed.
Have you experienced these symptoms of restlessness and difficulty focusing your entire life, or did they start at some point later on?

I think it’s been pretty much all along, not something that just showed up later. I mean, back in grade school, my teachers used to say I was bright but scattered. I was always misplacing pencils—funny how that sticks in my mind—and calling out answers before I was supposed to. They’d have to remind me to finish my work before running out to recess. So, yes, it goes way back.
Do you often feel like you're constantly on the go, even when you're not necessarily doing anything that requires a lot of physical activity?

Yeah… yes, I think that’s actually a big part of why I came in. Since I stopped working, I just don’t seem to slow down. I’ll be up and moving from one little job to the next all day, like I still have a crew waiting on me or something.

Even if it’s not anything important, I’ll be puttering around—start with one thing, then notice another—and before I know it I’ve been on my feet half the day. It’s strange, because there’s no boss calling, no schedule like there used to be, but my body still acts like there is.
Do you feel like your restlessness and difficulty focusing are causing problems in your daily life or relationships?

Yeah, I guess it is causing some problems. I don’t always like admitting that, but my wife has kind of had to take over the calendar—appointments, things I said I’d do, that sort of thing. She checks behind me more than she used to.

And I’ve had to apologize a few times, too, like to folks at the community center or the garden group, because I forgot something or didn’t follow through. Nothing huge, maybe, but enough that I feel bad about it.
Do you feel like your restlessness and difficulty focusing are causing you a lot of distress or anxiety?

I’m not sure I’d call it a lot of anxiety, exactly. Distress… maybe sometimes, when I realize I’ve dropped the ball on something. But I don’t sit around panicking over it.

It’s more like irritation with myself, if that makes sense. Like, I’ll be halfway through one thing and then—well, yesterday I went out to check the mail and ended up messing with the hose because it was kinked, and then I noticed the weeds by the fence… anyway, by the time I got back inside I’d forgotten what I meant to do. That kind of thing gets under my skin.

But “a lot of distress,” I don’t know. Maybe not a lot. Enough to be annoying.
Have you noticed your restlessness and difficulty focusing affecting your relationships with family or friends?

Yeah, it has, mostly at home. My wife’s had to kind of take over keeping the calendar and making sure I actually do the things I said I’d do. She’ll remind me, then remind me again, and I know that wears on her.

And with friends or groups… well, the community center and the garden group, I’ve had to apologize more than once because I let something slip or didn’t show up prepared. I don’t mean to let people down. I used to be pretty dependable, you know, back when I was working—well, I guess that’s not exactly the question—but yes, it does affect things a bit.
Have you ever had to quit a job or leave a social situation because of your restlessness or difficulty focusing?

I don’t think I’ve had to quit a job or leave a social thing outright because of it. I’m retired now, so the job part’s not really… well, not current.

But it has caused trouble. My wife has pretty much taken over the calendar and sort of checks behind me, because I’ll say I’ll do something and then it slips. And I’ve had to apologize to the community center and the garden group more than once for not following through. Like, I didn’t leave those situations, but I definitely let people down, and that doesn’t feel good.
Have you noticed your restlessness and difficulty focusing impacting your ability to maintain relationships or participate in activities you enjoy?

Yes, somewhat. I mean, I still go to things I enjoy, like the community center and the garden group, but I’ve had to apologize more than once because I dropped the ball or didn’t follow through.

And at home, my wife has kind of become the keeper of the calendar, which… she’s better at it anyway, but that’s not really fair to her. She’ll check behind me to make sure I didn’t forget something I said I’d do. So it hasn’t ruined relationships or anything, but it does put strain on them.
Have you noticed your restlessness and difficulty focusing affecting your ability to do things you need to do or to take care of yourself?

Yeah, I think so. Not so much the basic taking-care-of-myself stuff, but the things I’m supposed to keep track of—appointments, commitments, that sort of thing. My wife has kind of had to take over the calendar and check behind me, which I feel bad about.

And with the community center and the garden group—funny, the garden group has this whole sign-up sheet system now, which you’d think would help—but I’ve still let things slip more than once and had to apologize for letting people down. So yes, it affects getting things done, even if I don’t mean for it to.
Have you ever felt like your restlessness and difficulty focusing have significantly interfered with your ability to function in daily life or achieve your goals?

Yes, I’d say it has interfered, though I don’t know if I’d call it… I mean, I still get by day to day. But my wife has had to take over keeping the calendar and checking behind me, because otherwise things just slip through.

And I’ve had to apologize to the community center and the garden group more than once for letting people down. I like those places, too—the garden group especially, though I’m not much good with tomatoes, never have been—but anyway, yes, it gets in the way of doing what I mean to do.
Have you experienced these symptoms of restlessness and difficulty focusing in multiple settings throughout your life, such as at work, at home, and in social situations?

I’m not sure I can lay it out that neatly. I mean, at home, yes, my wife would probably have examples before I finished this sentence. Socially… maybe, but I don’t always notice it in the moment.

Work is harder to say, since I’m not working now. Back when I did, it’s all sort of mixed together in my memory—different bosses, different routines, you know how some places have better coffee than others and somehow that affects your whole day. So I guess I’d say it shows up in more than one place, but I’d need you to maybe narrow down what you mean.
Do you think your difficulty focusing is the main reason you have trouble completing tasks, or is it more that you just don't feel like doing them?

It’s more the focusing and following through, I think. I don’t usually start out thinking, “I don’t want to do this.”

Like my wife might ask me to fix the gate, sweep the porch, and put the tools away, and I’ll start on the gate… then I notice weeds by the fence and somehow I’m pulling those instead. Next thing you know the gate’s only half done and the tools are still sitting out. I mean, the weeds needed doing too, I suppose, but that wasn’t what I was asked to finish.
Did you experience significant restlessness and difficulty focusing as a child, similar to what you're experiencing now?

Yes, I think so. Even in grade school, teachers would say I was bright but scattered—my mother used to repeat that phrase, “bright but scattered,” like it was written on my report cards.

I was always losing pencils, calling out answers before I was supposed to, needing reminders to finish my work before recess. Recess was a big motivator, of course—kickball and all that—but even then I’d sort of drift off or rush ahead and miss what I was meant to finish. So yes, it goes back pretty far.
Do you think your main problem is paying attention and staying focused, or is it more about feeling restless and impulsive?

I’d say the restless part is what’s really been getting my attention lately. The focus is there too, sure, but what brought me in is more that since I stopped working, I just can’t seem to slow down.

I’m up and moving from one little job to the next all day, like I still have a crew waiting on me or a foreman coming around the corner. I’ll think, “I should just sit for a minute,” and then I’m already checking something in the garage or picking up a tool or starting some small thing outside. It’s not even always important, it’s just… I keep going.
Have you ever felt like your symptoms have caused significant problems in your relationships or daily life?

Yes… yes, I’d say it has. I don’t like admitting that, because it sounds like I’m blaming everything on this, but my wife has pretty much had to take over the calendar for us. Appointments, birthdays, when we’re supposed to be somewhere—she keeps track, and then she’ll check behind me too, like whether I actually did what I said I’d do.

And outside the house, too. I help with the community center sometimes, and the garden group—well, I try to. Nice bunch of people, actually, they do a plant sale in the spring and somebody always brings those little lemon cookies—anyway, I’ve had to apologize more than once because I forgot something or didn’t follow through and people were counting on me. So yes, it’s caused some problems. Not huge disasters, but enough that it’s embarrassing.
Do you think your difficulty with restlessness and feeling constantly on the go is more bothersome to you than your difficulty with focusing and completing tasks?

Yes, I think the being constantly on the go is more bothersome right now. Since I stopped working, it’s like I don’t have that natural structure anymore, but my body still thinks I’m supposed to be doing something every minute.

I’ll go from one little job to another all day—garage, yard, checking this, fixing that—like there’s still a crew waiting on me somewhere. Which is funny, because there isn’t, of course. Nobody’s standing there with a clipboard. But I feel like I can’t slow down, and that’s what made me think, “Alright, maybe I should talk to somebody about this.”

Appointments, birthdays, when we’re supposed to be somewhere—she keeps track, and then she’ll check behind me too, like whether I actually did what I said I’d do.

And outside the house, too. I help with the community center sometimes, and the garden group—well, I try to. Nice bunch of people, actually, they do a plant sale in the spring and somebody always brings those little lemon cookies—anyway, I’ve had to apologize more than once because I forgot something or didn’t follow through and people were counting on me. So yes, it’s caused some problems. Not huge disasters, but enough that it’s embarrassing.

doctor.intent: Determine if symptoms are predominantly inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive
doctor.question: Do you think your difficulty with restlessness and feeling constantly on the go is more bothersome to you than your difficulty with focusing and completing tasks?

target_item.name: Constant_Activity
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that since I stopped working, I can’t seem to slow down—I’m up and moving from one little job to the next all day like I still have a crew waiting on me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is most directly asking whether the feeling of being constantly on the go is the more bothersome symptom, which matches this item.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think the being constantly on the go is more bothersome right now. Since I stopped working, it’s like I don’t have that natural structure anymore, but my body still thinks I’m supposed to be doing something every minute.

I’ll go from one little job to another all day—garage, yard, checking this, fixing that—like there’s still a crew waiting on me somewhere. Which is funny, because there isn’t, of course. Nobody’s standing there with a clipboard. But I feel like I can’t slow down, and that’s what made me think, “Alright, maybe I should talk to somebody about this.”

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms of restlessness, difficulty focusing, impulsivity, and excessive physical activity have been present since childhood and are causing significant problems in daily life and relationships, which is consistent with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive Type.
